title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
statement: There are n cities and a list of one-way flights [from, to, price]. Find the cheapest price to get from src to dst using at most k stops in between. A trip with k stops uses k + 1 flights. Return -1 if no such trip exists.

example.caption: From city 0 to city 3 with at most 1 stop. 0, 1, 3 costs 700. The cheaper 0, 1, 2, 3 (400) needs two stops, so it is not allowed.

idea.sentence: Run k + 1 rounds, where round r finds the best price using at most r flights, and in each round read prices from a copy of the previous round.

jargon.plain: Go over every edge again and again, lowering a node's cost when an edge gives a cheaper way. After r passes, costs are correct for paths of at most r edges.
A city you land in between the start and the goal. k stops means k + 1 flights.
If cost[from] + price beats cost[to], update cost[to].

compare.bruteLabel: Try every route up to k+1 flights
compare.unit: steps (rough; routes can grow like m^(k+1), and nm stands for (k+1) * m)

rows.name: Try every route
rows.note: Follow every flight sequence of at most k+1 flights and keep the cheapest that reaches dst.

rows.name: Bellman-Ford, k+1 rounds
rows.note: Each round touches every flight once. Only two cost arrays are alive.

rows.name: Dijkstra on (city, flights used)
rows.note: Not shown. Works, but the state must include flights used, so plain Dijkstra on cities is wrong.

fast.takeaway: Plain Dijkstra ignores the stop limit. Bellman-Ford rounds count flights for free, but only if every round reads a frozen copy.

stages.title: Start
stages.note: Cost to src is 0, everything else infinity. This is the situation with zero flights.

stages.title: Copy for the round
stages.note: Make next as a copy of cost. The round reads cost and writes next.

stages.title: Add one flight
stages.note: For each flight, if cost[from] + price beats next[to], update next[to]. Reading cost keeps it to one extra flight.

stages.title: Answer
stages.note: After k + 1 rounds read cost[dst]. If it is still infinity, return -1.

edges.title: k = 0, direct flight only
edges.why: One round means one flight. The cheap two-flight route through city 1 is not allowed.

edges.title: Cheaper route needs too many stops
edges.input: chain 0-1-2-3-4 at 1 each, plus 0 to 4 at 10, k=2
edges.why: The chain costs 4 but needs 4 flights. With k=2 only 3 flights are allowed, so the direct 10 wins.

edges.title: No route
edges.why: City 2 stays at infinity. Return -1, not the infinity value.

edges.title: Parallel flights
edges.why: Both flights are checked. The second one lowers the cost from 5 to 2.

gotchas.text: Update in place and a single round can chain several flights, because a later flight sees the price the earlier one just wrote. The stop limit is silently ignored. Always write to a copy.
Do not run Dijkstra on cities alone. The cheapest way to a city may use too many flights, while a pricier way with fewer flights is the one you need later.
cost.slice() is a shallow copy, which is enough for a flat number array. For a 2-D table you would also have to copy every row.
Infinity is fine for comparing costs, but JSON turns it into null. Never put raw Infinity into anything you display or send.
math.MaxInt + price overflows to a negative number and would beat every real cost. Check cost[from] != math.MaxInt before adding.
next := cost would only copy the slice header, so both names would share one array. Use slices.Clone (or make + copy).

recap.key: Round r holds the best prices using at most r flights, built by reading the previous round's copy.
moves: Each of k + 1 rounds: copy cost into next
For every flight, relax next[to] using cost[from]
Swap, repeat, then return cost[dst] or -1
